subject: physics

turns.reply: Welcome! Let's start with something from everyday life: when you press the button on a torch and the bulb lights up, what do you think is going on inside it to make that happen?

turns.student: idk like... electricity goes in somehow?
turns.reply: That's fine, you're on the right track: something does travel through the wires. It's tiny particles that carry charge, and they drift round together. What do you think would happen to the bulb if there were a gap in the wire?

turns.student: umm the particles would just jump across the gap?
turns.reply: Not quite. The particles can't jump across a gap, so the flow stops everywhere in the loop and the bulb goes out. Where else in a torch might a gap like that appear when you slide it to off?
Not quite: a gap in the battery isn't how a torch switches off. The gap opens in the switch itself, where it breaks the loop so nothing can flow round.
A switch is the part that opens or closes a gap in the wire, to stop or start the flow. Think of the light switch on your bedroom wall. What do you do with it to make the light stop working?

turns.student: flip it down to break the wire
turns.reply: Yes: flipping the switch down opens a gap in the circuit, so nothing gets round and the light stops.

The amount of charge that passes a point is called the charge flow, and it is counted in coulombs (C). Picture the running track: the charge flow is how many runners go past one spot. What part of the track would you stand at to count them?

turns.student: anywhere on the track really? like by the finish line?
turns.reply: Yes, anywhere works, the finish line included. In a single loop the same amount of charge passes every spot each second, so the count is the same wherever you stand.
before: First, a word you'll need: **work**. The transfer of energy by a force

turns.student: so like more runners means more charge flow right
turns.reply: Yes, more runners passing a spot means more charge flow, counted in coulombs (C). Suppose 3 coulombs pass the finish line, then 4 more pass a little later. What is the total charge flow in coulombs?

A coulomb (C) is the unit we count charge in, like counting runners one by one. And 7 coulombs is right: 3 plus 4 gives 7. Now suppose 10 coulombs passed the finish line, and 2 more passed the same spot.

Yes, 12 coulombs is right: 10 plus 2 gives the charge flow, the total charge passing a point. We write charge flow as Q, so here Q = 12 C.

Now suppose 5 coulombs pass the finish line in one second, then 5 more pass in the next second. What is Q after those two seconds?

Sorry, that was a lot. Simply: charge flow, Q, is just the total number of coulombs that go past a spot, like counting all the runners who cross the finish line.

Suppose 4 coulombs cross the finish line, then 6 more cross. What is Q in coulombs?
Yes — 10 coulombs is right, because you added the two amounts of charge together.

turns.student: cool so Q is just adding up the charge yeah
turns.reply:
Yes, Q is the total charge that passes a point, counted in coulombs. Now the next idea: if charge passes steadily, the current is how much passes each second, so 3 coulombs passing every second is a current of 3 amps.

If 3 coulombs pass each second, what is Q after 2 seconds, in coulombs?

turns.student: idk how to work that out
turns.reply:
That's okay, let's do it in steps. If 3 coulombs cross the finish line in the first second, then another 3 coulombs cross in the second second, you just add them up like before.

How many coulombs have crossed after those 2 seconds?

Yes — 6 coulombs is right, because you added 3 and 3. A coulomb is just the unit we count charge in.

If 3 coulombs pass each second, how many coulombs have passed after 3 seconds?
Yes, 9 coulombs is right, because 3 coulombs pass each second, and adding 3 three times gives the total after 3 seconds.

turns.student: got it so i just keep adding
turns.reply: Yes, just keep adding. The amount of charge that has passed a point is called the charge flow, written Q, and it's counted in coulombs. Say 4 coulombs pass each second.
Now try it the other way round: 4 coulombs pass a point each second, and that steady flow lasts for 5 seconds. How many coulombs of charge flow have passed after those 5 seconds?

Yes, 20 coulombs is right, and a coulomb is just the unit we use to count charge. Multiplying works because 4 coulombs pass each second for 5 seconds. Now suppose the flow was only 2 coulombs each second, still for 5 seconds.

Yes, 10 coulombs is right: 2 coulombs each second for 5 seconds. A coulomb is just the unit we count charge in. Notice the flow was smaller this time, so less charge passed.

Now suppose the flow is 3 coulombs each second, for 4 seconds. How many coulombs pass?
That's fine, I haven't shown you the way to work it out yet, so let's build it step by step.

turns.student: um is it 3 plus 4 equals 7 coulombs?
turns.reply:
Not quite. A coulomb is the unit we count charge in, and here 3 and 4 are multiplied, not added: 3 coulombs pass each second, and that happens for 4 seconds.

So how many coulombs pass in total?
That's fine, I haven't given you the numbers yet, so there was nothing to work from. Let's go back to the start and take it one step at a time.

Being hungry is fair, and you can come back to this any time. Charge flow, Q, is how much charge passes a point, counted in coulombs (C). If 3 coulombs pass a point every second, how many coulombs have passed after 2 seconds?

Yes, 3 times 2 is 6 coulombs, so you multiplied the charge each second by the seconds. That "how much charge passes each second" is called electric current, and we measure it in amperes (A), so 1 ampere is 1 coulomb each second.

turns.reply:
Electric current is a flow of charge, and its size is how much charge passes a point each second, measured in amperes (A). Like runners passing a marker on a track: the more runners passing each second, the bigger the current.

If 5 coulombs pass a point every second, what is the current in amperes?

Yes, 5 amperes is right: 5 coulombs each second means a current of 5 A. An ammeter is the meter that measures current in amperes.

If an ammeter reads 4 A, how many coulombs pass that point each second?
Yes, 4 coulombs each second is right. Coulombs are the unit of charge, so 4 A means 4 coulombs pass that point every second.

turns.student: so current is just coulombs per second basically?
turns.reply: Yes, that's the idea: current is how many coulombs, the unit of charge, pass a point each second.
One ampere is one coulomb passing each second, so a current of 2 A means 2 coulombs pass each second. If an ammeter reads 3 A, how many coulombs pass that point in 1 second?

Yes, 3 coulombs each second is right, because 3 A means 3 coulombs pass every second. Charge only flows round a closed circuit, which is a complete loop with no gaps, like a running track you can lap. If you cut the wire so there is a gap in the loop, what happens to the current?

A closed circuit is a complete loop with no gaps. Charge only flows round it if it also has a cell in it to push the charge along. If you took the cell out, leaving a gap, what would happen to the lamp?
before: First, a word you'll need: **lamp**. In a circuit, a bulb is called a lamp.
First, a word you'll need: **cell**. Something that pushes charge round a circuit.

turns.reply: Yes: the lamp would turn off, because a gap means the loop is broken, so no charge can get round.

A closed circuit is a complete loop, and charge only flows round it if there's a cell in the loop to push it. Picture a loop with a lamp and a cell, then a loop with a lamp and no cell. In which loop does the lamp light?
Think of a loop with a lamp, and a cell as the thing that pushes. No push, no flow. Suppose you build a complete loop with a lamp but forget to put in a cell.

turns.student: the lamp wont light cos no cell to push
turns.reply: Yes: no cell means no push, so no flow. A closed circuit is a complete loop, and charge flows round it only if the loop also has a cell to push it. Suppose you join a cell into the loop but cut the wire somewhere. What happens to the lamp?

turns.student: lamp turns off cos the loop is broken
turns.reply: Yes — breaking the loop stops the flow, so the lamp goes off. An ammeter is the meter that measures current, and it goes inside the loop, in line with the lamp, so the charge flows through it.
flags: no question on a teaching turn

turns.student: so ammeter measures how bright the lamp is?
turns.reply:
Not quite. An ammeter doesn't measure brightness; it measures current, which is how much charge flows round the loop each second.

Suppose you move the ammeter to a different spot in the same single loop. What does it still measure?
That's fine, not knowing is okay. It still measures the current, meaning how much charge is flowing past a point each second.

turns.student: ok so current is same everywhere in the loop?
turns.reply:
Yes, in a single loop the current is the same at every point, because charge is not used up on the way round.

Picture the running track: if 3 runners pass the start line each second, how many pass the far side of the track each second?

turns.student: 3 runners pass the far side each second
turns.reply: Yes, 3 runners pass the far side each second, because the same runners keep going round the loop, so the rate is the same everywhere on the track.

Rate means how quickly something happens: how many times it happens each second. For current, it's how many pieces of charge pass a point each second.

On the running track, what would happen to the rate if 6 runners passed the start line each second instead of 3?

turns.student: 6 runners would pass the far side each second
turns.reply: Not quite — the rate would go up to 6 runners each second, because the rate is how many pass a point every second, and it was 3 before.

turns.student: so if current goes up the rate goes up too?
turns.reply:
Yes. Current is the rate of flow of charge, so if more charge passes a point each second, the current is bigger.

On the track, if 2 runners pass each second, what happens to the current if 5 runners pass each second instead?
Yes — the current goes up, because more runners (more charge) pass each second.

turns.student: im so hungry rn can we take a break
turns.reply:
That's fine, you can come back to this lesson any time. If you carry on, here's one more bit: an ammeter is the meter that measures current, and it goes in the loop itself, in line with the lamp.

If the ammeter sits in the loop, which unit does it show the current in?
An ammeter is just a meter that measures current, and it goes right in the loop with the lamp.
Yes — amperes (amps) is right, that's the unit of current. Because the current is the same everywhere in a single loop, the ammeter can go anywhere in it.

turns.student: yeah im gonna go eat something bye
turns.reply: No problem, thanks for sticking with it. Today you answered questions on electric current. Your place is saved, so we'll pick up right here next time. Bye for now!
